sentences.text: This is part four of our lecture on state assignment.
Last time, the ring of five did nothing until we set it into a used state.
That ring spent two more flip-flops than it needed, mostly for fun.
This part is about a style that spends flip-flops just as freely, and is used a lot in real designs.
Here are eight states, built two ways.
On the right, three flip-flops count through them in binary.
On the left, eight flip-flops pass a single one along, one flip-flop for each state.
That's eight flip-flops where three would do.
So what do we gain by giving every state its own flip-flop?
This style is called one-hot encoding.
It's a shift-register style of design, in which only one flip-flop at a time holds a one.
That flip-flop is the hot one.
As the machine steps from state to state, the one steps from flip-flop to flip-flop.
You've seen something close to this.
Part two's ring of five carried a pair of ones round.
A one-hot machine always carries exactly one.
So each state has its own flip-flop, and the state is simply wherever the one is.
To see which state the machine is in, you just look for the one.
A sequential assignment needs only log base two of the number of states, rounded up.
One-hot needs one flip-flop for every state.
For eight states, that's eight flip-flops instead of three.
In the lecturer's words, here we really are burning through the flip-flops.
So why would anyone design this way?
The slide's answer is that one-hot can give simple, fast state machines.
And each output comes from joining the outputs of the right flip-flops, the ones for the states where it should be on, with an or gate.
Let's test both claims on a machine you already know.
The lecturer goes back to the traffic light from part one.
It steps through four states in the British order: red, then red and amber, then green, then amber, and back to red.
It has no inputs, and it moves on one state at every edge of the clock.
Four states, so one-hot needs four flip-flops, one for each state.
Call them the red, red-and-amber, green and amber flip-flops.
This time each one stands for a state, not a lamp.
In part one, these states had three-bit codes.
Now each code has a single one, in that state's own flip-flop.
Red is one, zero, zero, zero, red and amber is zero, one, zero, zero, and so on.
In the transition table, each state's next state is the next row down, and amber goes back to red.
Four flip-flops give sixteen patterns, and only four are used.
That leaves twelve unused states, or as the slide says, lots.
Now read the dee inputs off the table.
With dee flip-flops, they're just the next state.
The next-state column for red-and-amber reads one, zero, zero, zero, exactly the current red column.
So the red-and-amber flip-flop's input is the red flip-flop's output.
In the same way, green takes its input from red-and-amber, amber from green, and red from amber.
That's a ring of four, a shift register fed back on itself, and it needs no logic at all to work out the next state.
It has the same shape as part two's ring of five, but it carries a single one.
The flip-flops now say which state we're in, but there are four flip-flops and only three lamps.
The red lamp is on in two states, red and red-and-amber.
So it should light when either the red flip-flop or the red-and-amber flip-flop holds the one.
An or gate joins those two outputs.
The amber lamp is on in red-and-amber and in amber, so another or gate joins those two flip-flops.
The green lamp is on only in the green state.
It's simply the green flip-flop's output, a plain wire.
That's the slide's rule at work.
Each output joins the flip-flops of the states where it's on.
Here's the whole circuit, as the slide draws it.
Four dee flip-flops share one clock signal.
Each output is wired to the next input, and the last one runs back to the first.
Underneath are the two or gates and the wire for green.
As the one goes round, the lamps follow, red, then red and amber, then green, then amber.
So the next-state logic is gone, but we do need a little output logic, two gates.
Now compare lecture nine's design.
It used part one's codes, with three flip-flops, one per lamp.
The red lamp's flip-flop is fed by an exclusive-or gate, which takes the red and amber outputs.
The amber lamp's flip-flop takes its own inverted output, so amber simply flips on every edge of the clock.
The green lamp's flip-flop gets an and gate, fed by the red and amber outputs, because green always follows the one state with both of them lit.
And each lamp is driven straight from one of the flip-flops, so there's no output logic.
Put the two side by side.
Lecture nine's design needs two gates between its flip-flops.
One-hot needs none there, and two gates after them, for the lamps.
So the logic hasn't vanished, it has moved from inside the loop to the outputs.
Same machine, same lamps.
Only the state assignment changed.
Both designs go on the scoreboard.
Lecture nine's has three flip-flops, two next-state gates and no output logic.
One-hot has four flip-flops, no next-state gates, and two output gates.
Which is better depends on what you optimise, as part one said.
The lecturer built this circuit in his simulator.
The clock signal ticks, and nothing lights up.
Can you see why?
It's the same deal as the ring of five.
The flip-flops start at all zeros, and all zeros is an unused state, because a one-hot state has exactly one flip-flop at one.
So every edge of the clock shifts zeros into zeros.
First he disconnects the clock signal, so that nothing shifts while he works.
Any single one would make a used state.
He picks the amber flip-flop and pulls its asynchronous set input low.
Remember, the little circle means active low.
Its output goes to one, and the amber lamp lights at once, through its or gate.
Then he puts the set input back high, so the flip-flop works normally again.
He reconnects the clock signal, and the lights run.
Amber, red, red and amber, green, amber.
Like the ring of five, this ring can never find its own way back, because any pattern just goes round.
Its sixteen patterns fall into six loops, and only one of them is ours.
Power it up with two ones that have a gap between them, and the lamps alternate for ever between red with amber, and red with green.
So a one-hot machine has to start in a used state.
The lecturer's last point is speed.
Remember from lecture eight what limits the clock speed.
Every path runs from one flip-flop, through logic, to the next.
So the clock period must cover the clock-to-output delay, the logic's delay, and the set-up time.
Now look at the one-hot ring.
Each output is wired straight into the next input.
There's no logic in the loop, so the logic's delay is zero.
The clock period only has to cover the clock-to-output delay and the set-up time.
With lecture eight's flip-flops, that's zero point two plus zero point one, which is zero point three nanoseconds.
That's a clock frequency of about three point three gigahertz, as fast as these flip-flops can go.
In lecture eight's example, four point seven nanoseconds of logic held the clock to two hundred megahertz.
Here the flip-flops alone set the limit.
The or gates for the lamps sit after the loop.
They delay the lamps a little, but the clock never waits for them.
Lecture nine's design has two gates inside its loop, an and gate and an exclusive-or gate, so its clock period must also cover the slower of the two.
One more check from lecture eight.
With no logic between flip-flops, new data reaches the next input as early as it possibly can.
That's the hold-time worry, in the shift register's case, and flip-flops are normally designed to meet it.
So, in the lecturer's words, one-hot machines can be fast, but we could end up burning lots of flip-flops.
Let's recap.
In one-hot encoding, exactly one flip-flop holds a one, so there's one flip-flop per state.
Built one-hot, the traffic light is a ring of four, with no next-state logic at all.
Its lamps come from two or gates and one plain wire.
Compared with lecture nine's design, the logic moved out of the loop and onto the outputs.
Like any ring, it has to be set into a used state, here with an asynchronous set.
And with no logic in its loop, it runs as fast as its flip-flops allow.
Next time, a real machine with inputs, from a Cambridge exam question.
We'll build it the usual way, with two flip-flops, and then one-hot.
